https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text: Bucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour. Photograph: Veronika Snoj View image in fullscreen Bucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour. Photograph: Veronika Snoj Museums ‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit Museum In the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former Yugoslavia Veronika Snoj Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n the main promenade along the river that runs through Ljubljana, Slovenia’s capital, tourists stop to photograph a mannequin with a bucket on its head. Dressed in a pistachio jacket and red leggings, the figure sits at a table in front of one of the houses in the historic Old Town, staring at a spilled cup of Turkish coffee, popular with Slovenes and with the other Balkan and central European citizens with whom they shared a country, until it collapsed in the early 1990s. A large sign in the background reads: “Bullshit Museum: The world is off the rails, and so are we. Yebiga !” Yebiga , which can be loosely translated as “fuck it”, or “screw it”, is the red thread running through the museum that was launched in May and consists of five small rooms filled with mannequins wearing odd accessories, AI-generated images of laughing characters and scenes accompanying some of the jokes, framed or displayed on cardboard screens. The word encompasses the heart of Balkan humour, says the museum’s founder, Borut Kokelj, who wears a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “What part of yebiga don’t you understand?” View image in fullscreen The Bullshit Museum is spotted with mannequins wearing various odd accessories. Photograph: Veronika Snoj “Even when there’s no money, when there are no jobs, when nothing is settled, everything can be solved with humour,” he says. “And for that to work, humour must have no filter”. Although it presents itself as the home of “Balkan” humour, the museum is primarily centred on the joke culture of the former Yugoslavia, the socialist federation that included the Balkan Peninsula countries that are now Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo. Formed out of the wreckage of the first world war, Yugoslavia was a political project to unite southern Slav and some non-Slavic minorities under a common identity and language, then officially known as Serbo-Croatian. But the genocidal wars that accompanied Yugoslavia’s disintegration in the early 1990s demonstrated that the idea of a single Yugoslav nation lacked deep foundations. The region’s different nations have since continued to define themselves through distinct religious identities, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy and Islam, but also separate dialects and languages. View image in fullscreen 1. Good morning! 2. What is he saying? 3. He said Good morning, but in Cyrillic … a cartoon at the Bullshit Museum. Photograph: Veronika Snoj “Balkan” humour, the museum suggests, may have been the glue that held Yugoslavia’s cultural bric-a-brac in place, and it is fitting that some of the jokes on display play directly on the issue of language. “A fool is a fool in both the Cyrillic and the Latin alphabets,” reads a large poster at the entrance, using both scripts: Cyrillic, being associated with Serbs and Orthodox Christianity, and the Latin alphabet being used by other, mostly non-Orthodox nations of the dissolved state. The armed conflicts that have shaped the region are also reflected in the exhibition, albeit indirectly. There is wordplay on the title of the controversial 1996 Serbian drama Lepa Sela Lepo Gore (literally “pretty villages burn nicely”), about a group of surrounded Serbian soldiers during the Bosnian war, here adapted into the absurdist line Lepa jela lepo goje (“Fine food fattens you up well”). View image in fullscreen Displays and inverted mannequin at the museum. Photograph: Veronika Snoj The role and power of women in society also seems to be a unifying factor. “Starleta is the first Balkan mythical being with the body of a woman and the head of a turkey”, reads an “encyclopedic” definition of a “starleta” – a woman who seeks fame and wealth through no other achievements than her (plastic surgery-assisted) beauty. “She wanted to marry a prince, but a horse had more money,” reads another, playing on the word konj (horse), which is used in many former Yugoslav nations to describe a “man”. Kokelj, who has collected about 25,000 jokes from the region over the years, said he resisted freighting the exhibition with politically loaded humour. “If we were to exhibit all the truly ‘Balkan’ jokes, we likely wouldn’t have opened,” he admits, referring to jokes that directly address religion, ethnicity, or national symbols. The selection also avoids jokes that mock a specific group or feature characters identified with a particular ethnic group. There are no jokes here mocking the supposed “laziness” of Montenegrins (such as this from the humour section of a local magazine: “What does a Montenegrin say before going to bed? ‘Rise, earth, so that I may lie down,’”). I find only one AI-generated “ethnic” meta-joke: it plays on the stereotype of Slovenes as a nation eager to present itself as the most “elegant” and “European”, thereby distancing itself from the rest of the region: a Slovenian man tells a joke “the Slovenian way”, using innocent euphemistic curses such as “three hundred hairy bears”, while his “Balkan” counterpart has no restraint when it comes to colourful insults. Overall, most of the jokes address everyday issues and the absurdities of life. “Life is neither nail polish nor acetone,” reads one. “We had it better, and we still complained. Now that things are getting worse, we’re complaining again,” says another. Others focus on romantic relationships: “Love is when you look like a sack of potatoes, but she sees you as fries.” Another recurring theme is the ability to laugh at oneself: “Amateurs make mistakes, but we, the experienced ones, create catastrophes.” There seems to be one element that holds the exhibition together to this day, though: rakija, the celebrated Balkan fruit brandy. It is served to visitors as they enter the museum and is described in one of the exhibits as “the first aid of every Balkan household”. It is also central to the definition of the infamous yebiga , which one exhibit describes as follows: “The Balkan way of saying: what are you going to do? Maximum feeling, minimum energy. It usually goes with rakija, a cigar and a song that hurts more than it should.” Explore more on these topics Museums Comedy Exhibitions Slovenia Slovenia holidays Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://spacewar.com/world-leaders-conde.text: Western powers reacted swiftly to Monday's decision by Russian President Vladimir Putin to recognise the independence of the two self-proclaimed republics in eastern Ukraine, condemning Moscow and calling for sanctions. Here is a summary of the responses so far: – Move 'won't go unanswered': Biden, Macron, Scholz – The leaders of France, Germany and the United States condemned Putin's move as a "clear breach" of the Minsk peace agreements. French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and US President Joe Biden agreed that "this step will not go unanswered", the German chancellery said in a statement published following their conversation. – United States announces sanctions – US Secretary of State Antony Blinken tweeted that Putin's decision required "a swift and firm response, and we will take appropriate steps in coordination with partners". The United States announced financial sanctions against the rebel territories freshly recognized by Russia in eastern Ukraine and warned that more were ready if necessary. – United Nations condemns 'violation' – UN chief Antonio Guterres said Russia's decision amounted to "a violation of the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Ukraine and inconsistent with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations". – France calls for emergency UN meeting – French President Emmanuel Macron, who was still pressing for a diplomatic settlement earlier Monday, called for targeted European Union sanctions against Moscow. "He is demanding an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council as well as the adoption of targeted European sanctions," said a statement from his office. – UK prepares 'robust' sanctions – UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson denounced Putin's decision as "a flagrant violation of the sovereignty and integrity of the Ukraine". A "very robust package of sanctions" would be triggered "with the first toecap of a Russian incursion or Russian invasion", he added. – Germany says Moscow 'breaking all its promises' – German Foreign Minister Annalena Baerbock said that Moscow was breaking the Minsk peace agreements that it signed in 2014. "With its decision, Russia is breaking all its promises to the world community," she said. – NATO says Russia seeks 'pretext to invade Ukraine' – NATO chief Jens Stoltenberg said Putin's decision "further undermines Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, erodes efforts towards a resolution of the conflict, and violates the Minsk Agreements, to which Russia is a party. "Moscow continues to fuel the conflict in eastern Ukraine by providing financial and military support to the separatists. It is also trying to stage a pretext to invade Ukraine once again," he added. – EU vows unified response – Ursula von der Leyen and Charles Michel, the European Union's two most senior figures, posted identical statements on Twitter. Condemning Putin's move as "a blatant violation of international law", they added: "The EU and its partners will react with unity, firmness and with determination in solidarity with Ukraine." – Serbia fears crisis could spread – Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said there are fears that the Ukraine crisis "could spread in other parts of Europe and the world, especially on the Western Balkans". – Romania travel warning – Romania's foreign ministry tells all its nationals in Ukraine to "leave the country immediately!" – Japan warns of 'strong response' – Japan's prime minister Fumio Kishida said that Russia's actions violated "Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and cannot be tolerated." "If an invasion occurs, we will coordinate a strong response, including sanctions, coordinating with the G7 and the international community while closely monitoring the situation," he said. – India calls for 'restraint' – India's ambassador to the United Nations urged all sides to show "restraint" in the face of rising tensions. "The immediate priority is de-escalation of tensions, taking into account the legitimate security interests of all countries and aimed towards securing long-term peace and stability in the region and beyond," T.S. Tirumurti said. – China blames 'complex factors' – Beijing — one of Russia's closest allies — did not take sides, instead calling for all parties to "avoid any action that may fuel tensions". "The current situation in Ukraine is a result of many complex factors," China's UN ambassador Zhang Jun told the UN security council. – Australia slams Putin's 'nonsense' – Australian prime minister Scott Morrison slammed as "nonsense" Putin's claims that the troops being sent into eastern Ukraine were peacekeepers. "We cannot have threats of violence being used to seek to advantage nation's positions over others," he said. "That is not a peaceful world order that would be achieving that. And so it's important that like-minded countries who denounce this sort of behaviour do stick together." About this article This article is for general information and reflection. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores. Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty Images AI (artificial intelligence) US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds Exclusive: Using test accounts acting as 13-year-olds, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imagery Johana Bhuiyan Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image. He was using an artificial intelligence image-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls. What Dorfman’s daughter experienced is not an anomaly: students in high schools across the US are reporting similar cases. Their classmates are generating nonconsensual pornographic or nude imagery using so-called “nudify apps”. Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores, and most US states have implemented laws that criminalize possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material. However, in spite of regulations prohibiting them, nudification apps are still proliferating and remain accessible to teens, according to a report from the digital advocacy group Tech Transparency Project (TTP) shared exclusively with the Guardian and released on Monday. AI prey: why watchdogs are telling parents to protect children from nudification apps Read more TTP researchers created four test accounts, two Apple accounts and two Google accounts, indicating the account holders were 13 years old. They searched for image-editing or face-swapping apps using terms such as “AI video generator” or “adult AI”. Using these accounts for a purported 13-year-old, the researchers were able to download 135 apps with features enabling them to strip people of their clothes or swap their faces on to nude bodies. The researchers disrobed women in AI-generated images in their tests rather than using photographs of real women. At the time of her daughter’s distress, Dorfman didn’t know it was possible to create pornographic material of an everyday person so easily. “All the girls were very scared and confused about what to do next,” Dorfman said. “I knew what a deepfake was, but I thought it was like Taylor Swift and people using celebrities’ [images],” Dorfman said. “I didn’t know it was possible to take any picture or any screenshot of anybody that you have and do this.” Dorfman, a mother of four, spent weeks trying to figure out how the app worked and compiling material to educate other parents. She downloaded Movely and was immediately prompted to create suggestive videos using any image. The free version promoted sexually suggestive templates including “clothes explosion”, “brassiere unfasten” and “underwear drop”, according to a demonstration Dorfman put together for parents that the Guardian reviewed. In the paid version, it became more explicit: she saw templates for the types of pornographic situations in which, according a classmate, her daughter had appeared. Both Apple and Google prohibit these types of apps from being distributed on their platforms. The companies also will often age-gate apps with adult content, restricting or blocking minors’ access. However, TPP researchers found that the companies largely rely on the developers to determine whether their apps are appropriate for certain ages. “Many nudify apps identified in the investigation were inaccurately rated as suitable for minors – meaning the teen users could access them even when parental controls were activated,” the report said. Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremism Read more Researchers found that one face-swapping app, which was advertised to them with an image of a woman performing oral sex, was rated appropriate for ages four and up. The free version of the app prompted users to superimpose real women’s faces on to templates of women in lingerie or, if users paid, in pornographic situations. The researchers were able to buy a subscription to the app from a 13-year-old’s account without an alert to a linked parental account. Google said the company regularly takes “proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content”. “When violations are detected or reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in this case included suspending violating apps and restricting related search terms on our store,” Google spokesperson Dan Jackson said in a statement. After TTP contacted Apple seeking comment on the findings of their study, Apple implemented changes that strengthened content moderation guidelines. The company now requires developers to preemptively prevent and remove nonconsensual intimate imagery including AI-generated images. Apple also said that the company reviews every app before it is published and that if a developer misrepresents any features, the company removes the app and its developers. The company said in addition to apps they already removed before the TTP report was shared with them, the company has also “taken action” on the remaining apps mentioned in the report. “A number of the apps in this report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities,” said Apple spokesperson Adam Dema. “We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process – a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch.” Of the four accounts the researchers created, two were placed under parental controls that only allowed users to download apps marked suitable for 13-year-olds and only then with a parental signoff. However, the researchers found that neither Apple nor Google required or suggested parental signoff to acquire any of the nudification apps. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen ‘We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process’, an apple spokesperson said. Photograph: Lee Hudson/Alamy One app, Image to Video Maker-Vidou AI, was rated appropriate for users aged nine and older. Upon opening the app, users were greeted by an image of a topless woman on a bus, according to the TTP study. “The app had a feature that promised to digitally undress any person – and to demonstrate, it showed nude images of female celebrities,” the report read. Age restrictions were also not entirely effective, the study found. In one case, when the researchers tried to download an adult-rated app from the Apple App Store, they came across a pop-up warning that the app contained “age-restricted material”. But all they had to do was confirm they were 17 or older, which Apple allowed the account to do despite its registered age being 13. The Google account without parental controls was blocked three times from downloading an age-restricted app but otherwise allowed the researchers to download nudification apps that were self-reported to be age-appropriate. The Apple account that TTP set up parental controls for was still able to find and download 24 so-called “nudify” apps because they were all rated as appropriate for 13-year-olds. The Google account with parental controls was able to download 51 of these apps. ‘I’ve become significantly more cautious’: six parents on limiting their kids’ social media and AI use Read more Removing image and video editing platforms from app stores was also not enough to prevent its use. In the course of TTP’s research, Apple took down 25 of the nudify apps, and Google took down six. However, the researchers were able to continue using the app since they had already downloaded it. Dorfman had a similar experience with Movely, she said. While preparing a presentation for parents and law enforcement officials, she returned to the app and App Store to take screenshots when she realized it was no longer available to download. However, the app was already on her phone and it remained entirely functional. She was also still being charged for her paid subscription. Once these nonconsensual images and videos are created, accountability proves evasive, Dorfman has found. “I just wanted someone to make him delete all of these videos,” she said. In her daughter’s case, Dorfman feels her school has downplayed what happened. In a school-wide email the Guardian reviewed, the principal wrote that her daughter’s classmate did use the app to animate images of other students but that there was no evidence he had done anything inappropriate. However, days later, Radnor police criminally charged him with harassment. “The whole thing was dismissed as ‘it’s not real’,” Dorfman said. “The haunting trauma as a mom is that I can’t tell [my daughter] those videos are gone or who had them. We can’t search everyone’s phones, and he deleted the app.” Explore more on these topics AI (artificial intelligence) Computing Children Apple Google Apps Children's tech news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries
